clue.text: Leading TV star's initial troubles

parts.note: a side that is leading is up, ahead in the game
a TV is a television set

indicators.note: the initial of a word is its opening letter, taken here from star's

explanation.surface: The first big name on a television show makes trouble early.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouble someone is to upset them; both verbs mean disturb or distress.

clue.text: Invader right to occupy island, said writer

indicators.note: one thing occupying another sits inside it, so the letter for right goes within

parts.note: John Donne wrote that no man is an island, so the poet's phrase gives no man

explanation.surface: A conqueror has a right to take an island, according to some author.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is John Donne, whose line 'No man is an island' is borrowed whole; 'said' points to his quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Normans conquered England in 1066, so a Norman is a classic invader.

clue.text: Enter uni after working for a time in office

indicators.note: something working is in action and so can be rearranged into a new order

parts.note: U is short for university, informally uni

explanation.surface: A student goes to university after a job, to spend a term in some post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges ENTER plus U; 'after' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenure is the period during which a post or position is held.

clue.text: Boisterous behaviour from eminent judge with tattoos

parts.note: an eminent figure is high in rank
J is the abbreviation for judge, as in legal titles
to tattoo someone is to ink them, so tattoos are inks

explanation.surface: A senior judge covered in tattoos is surprising enough to cause uproar.
explanation.definitionFit: High jinks is an idiom for rowdy, lively fun and horseplay.

clue.text: Glare irritated composer

indicators.note: letters that are irritated are stirred up, so the word glare is rearranged

explanation.surface: An annoyed stare from a musician.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Elgar was an English composer, of the Enigma Variations among much else.

clue.text: Harm old count locked in tower

indicators.note: a thing locked in another is enclosed by it, so these letters go inside the rest

parts.note: to harm something is to mar it
to tell is an old sense of count, as a bank teller counts money

explanation.surface: A villain does harm, an aged nobleman is imprisoned in a tower.
explanation.walkthrough: Count is the verb, as in telling votes, not a nobleman.
explanation.definitionFit: A Martello tower is a small round coastal fort built in Britain against Napoleon.

clue.text: Anti-UKIP — clear about a way for Brussels to get back on top

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece on top of another comes first
getting back means going in the reverse direction, so this street name is read backwards

parts.note: Brussels is French-speaking, and the French for street or way is rue

indicators.note: one word about another surrounds it

parts.note: something clear is plain and open

explanation.surface: An opponent of UKIP clears a route for the EU to regain the upper hand.
explanation.walkthrough: UKIP was the anti-EU UK Independence Party. Brussels speaks French, so its word for street is wanted; 'to get back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Opponents of UKIP were typically pro-European, so a European stance is anti-UKIP.

clue.text: Lad does wrong section — he's useless

indicators.note: letters set wrong are in the wrong order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boy performs part of a task badly and is called hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges LADDOES plus S.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead loss is an informal idiom for a person who is completely ineffective.

clue.text: Given backing on Tyneside

parts.note: someone backing a cause is pro it
Tyneside, around Newcastle, is in the North East of England, NE

explanation.surface: Something offered as support in the Newcastle area.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyneside is the Newcastle area in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Given and prone both mean inclined or liable to do something.

clue.text: True in all weathers (though it's never sunny)

indicators.note: weathering wears something away and changes its form, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A saying that something holds good whatever the weather, even with endless cloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weathers' rearranges TRUEINALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A sullen, grumpy disposition is the opposite of a sunny temperament.

clue.text: Old feature of English resort

parts.note: ex means former or old, as in an ex-partner
the mouth is one of the facial features

explanation.surface: A long-standing attraction of a seaside town in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Exmouth is a seaside town in Devon, south-west England.

clue.text: Design I had not like a flower

indicators.note: to design is to plan or arrange, so these letters are arranged anew

explanation.surface: Someone disowns a pattern that looked like a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Design' rearranges IHADNOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthoid is an adjective from Greek anthos, bloom, meaning resembling one.

clue.text: Idiot leaving church rinses face in font

indicators.note: an idiot jumbles things, so these letters are thrown into disorder
the church letters leaving a word means they are taken out of it

parts.note: CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: A fool walks out of church and washes his face in the font.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' takes CE from FACE to give FA; 'Idiot' rearranges RINSES plus FA. The church font is a typeface font.
explanation.definitionFit: A typeface without serifs is called sans serif, a style used for many fonts.

clue.text: In use around North, say

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run use around, spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A remark on using something near the north.
explanation.definitionFit: The North Sea is one example of a sea, hence the say.

clue.text: Black Death at its outset

parts.note: in the board game the victim, Dr Black, is found murdered before play begins

explanation.surface: The plague as it first broke out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Black Death was the 14th-century plague, but here Black is the murdered man in a board game.
explanation.definitionFit: In the detective board game the solvers investigate Dr Black's killing, which happens before the game opens.

clue.text: Parent upset by a smooth character (sharing with 7)

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the word is reversed

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
a in the sense of each, as in ten pounds a head, is per
to sand wood is to smooth it

explanation.surface: A mother annoyed by a slick person who has to share with someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: AM, then PER, then SAND. On a UK keyboard this symbol shares the 7 key.
explanation.definitionFit: The & symbol for and is a typographical character, typed with shift and 7.

clue.text: Recycling stock, this martyr

indicators.note: recycling sends letters round again, from one end of the word to the other

parts.note: a stock phrase is trite or banal

explanation.surface: Reusing supplies, as this saint did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recycling' moves the last two letters, AL, of BANAL to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Alban was the first recorded Christian martyr in Britain.

clue.text: Evangelists have drinks outside station

indicators.note: the drinks go outside, wrapping round the station word

parts.note: ales are drinks of beer
a post is a station, as in a guard at his post

explanation.surface: Preachers having a pint outside the railway station.
explanation.definitionFit: Apostles were early missionaries spreading the gospel, so evangelists in the broad sense.

clue.text: Respectful acknowledgement to courage I needed to spar

parts.note: a bow is a respectful gesture of greeting

indicators.note: needed is read as lacking, so the I is missing from the word

parts.note: spirit means courage or mettle

explanation.surface: A boxer bows to show respect before he must summon courage to fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needed' in the sense 'was without' drops I from SPIRIT. Spar is the noun, a ship's pole, not boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowsprit is a spar projecting from the bow of a sailing ship.

clue.text: Earl's nothing on, looking cold in shade

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: nil means nothing, zero
E is an abbreviation for earl
someone with cold skin looks blue

explanation.surface: A naked aristocrat turns blue sitting in the shade.
explanation.definitionFit: Nile blue is a pale greenish-blue colour, a shade.

clue.text: Pointless to just glance through novel

indicators.note: without a point of the compass, here the letter for south

parts.note: to skim a text is to glance through it

explanation.surface: It's pointless merely to flick through a new book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointless' removes S (south, a compass point) from SKIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudyard Kipling wrote the novel titled with this boy's name.

clue.text: Camels ugly? Not so

indicators.note: an ugly version is a misshapen form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether camels are ugly and gets a denial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ugly' rearranges NOTSO.
explanation.definitionFit: Oonts is an Anglo-Indian word for camels, used by Kipling.

clue.text: Zip up top — had contracted not to show a valuable commodity

parts.note: zip means nothing, zero, which looks like O

indicators.note: in a down entry up means the letters read from bottom to top
the letter that does not show is removed from the word

parts.note: a lid is a top
had shortened becomes 'd, the letter D

explanation.surface: Fasten the jacket; you'd agreed to skip work, a costly matter.
explanation.walkthrough: D is taken from LID, leaving LI, which 'up' turns to IL below O.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil, the crude extracted from wells, is a major traded commodity.

clue.text: Killer revolutionary breaking party rules

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns round, so the whole build is read backwards
the rules break into the party word, sitting inside it

parts.note: a do is a party
laws are rules

explanation.surface: An assassin, a rebel who flouts the party line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns round the whole assembly, not just one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Lee Harvey Oswald assassinated President Kennedy in 1963.

clue.text: Force to abandon mile-high bonking — caught interrupting so-called emergency procedure

indicators.note: the letter interrupting the rest goes inside them
bonking is a bash or bang, so these letters are knocked out of order
the letter for force abandons the word, being dropped

parts.note: G is the symbol for gravitational force
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A couple's in-flight romp is interrupted by an emergency.
explanation.walkthrough: MILEHIGH less G gives MILEHIH, rearranged as HEIMLIH; C goes before the last H. So-called because the procedure bears a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The Heimlich manoeuvre is a first-aid technique for clearing a choking person's airway.

clue.text: Doctor's intended not one to be flash

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a doctor

indicators.note: not means the letter for one is left out

parts.note: intended means meant
A is one, the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A doctor's plan was not to be showy.
explanation.definitionFit: In a flash means in an instant, so a flash is a very brief period of time.

clue.text: Annoying Annie's not a good idea

indicators.note: annoying means troubling or disturbing, so these letters are disturbed

parts.note: the name with its possessive s supplies all six letters

explanation.surface: Irritating Annie is a bad notion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annoying' rearranges ANNIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A crazy plan is foolish, so something mad is not a good idea.

clue.text: Girls endearingly 'hot' — payments upfront not required

parts.note: H stands for hot, as on taps

indicators.note: the upfront letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: moneys are sums paid

explanation.surface: Calling women 'hot' while the deposit is waived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upfront not required' drops M from MONEYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Honey is a term of endearment, so girls addressed fondly could be called this.

clue.text: Heard acting editor's dropping round

indicators.note: acting means performing, so the remaining letters put on a new show
the editor dropping the round thing means it is removed

parts.note: the word editor itself, its possessive giving nothing
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: The temporary editor is said to be calling on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' removes O from EDITOR; 'acting' rearranges EDITR.
explanation.definitionFit: A court that has heard a case has tried it, the legal sense of hearing.

clue.text: Swapping party — be back in for key attachment

indicators.note: the reversed word goes in the rest
swapping its two parts moves the front of the word to the end
back means the little word reads backwards

explanation.surface: At a wife-swapping party, someone is told to come back in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swapping' exchanges the word's two halves, giving TYPAR; 'back' turns be round, and it sits in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: On a typewriter a type bar is the lever carrying the letter, struck by each key.

clue.text: Flipping Cameron is disciple of Maggie? Possibly

indicators.note: flipping turns the words over, so they read from end to start

parts.note: David Cameron was PM, Prime Minister
a disciple can be called a son, a follower of a master

explanation.surface: Is the irritating Cameron a follower of Margaret Thatcher?
explanation.walkthrough: PM IS backwards is SIMP. 'Flipping' is also a British mild curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Maggie is the baby in the TV cartoon family, so she is one example.

clue.text: Menu defaced, I start to eat crap? Unlikely!

definitions.text: Menu defaced, I start to eat crap? Unlikely!

indicators.note: an unlikely arrangement is an improbable one, so these letters are reordered
the face, the front letter, is removed from the word
only the start of the word eat is kept, so its remaining letters are dropped

explanation.surface: A diner spoils the menu and says he might eat rubbish, but it's improbable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'defaced' leaves ENU; 'start to' cuts eat down to its opening E; 'Unlikely' rearranges ENU, I, E and CRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A gourmet devoted to fine food would hardly start eating rubbish.

clue.text: No Man City in Europe

definitions.meaning: a slang, offensive term for an effeminate man, one held not to be manly
a city in Lorraine, north-east France

explanation.surface: A football fan sneers at Manchester City's European record.
explanation.definitionFit: The French city is in Lorraine, and the slang word is an old insult for an unmanly male.
